The appellant was the sole executor of the will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, in favour of the respondent. The respondent was entitled only to a life interest in items 1 and 2 and that on her death the properties were to be disposed of by the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for possession of items 3, 4 and 5 and a declaration that the appellant was entitled to dispose of them by a will. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant filed a suit in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Mysore, for possession of the items of properties covered by the will under five items. The trial judge held that the appellant had failed to prove that the properties were in fact the properties of the respondent and that the appellant could not be entitled to dispose them by a valid will. The High Court, however, held that the will was not proved by the appellant, and that the will had been executed by her. The High court also held that the respondent was entitled to the properties in the hands of the appellant under the will. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the High Court was not justified in recording its findings on two other issues in the present proceedings. The High Courts were not justified in holding that the will did not amount to a valid will and that the High court was not justified to interfere with the findings of the trial court. The High 'Court was not justified, in recording its conclusions on two other points, in the present case, in reversing the finding of the trial Court and in reversing the findings of fact. The High. Court was not right in recording its finding on two other questions. The High, Court was not entitled to interfere with a finding of fact arrived at by the trial court on two other matters. The High Power of Attorney was not a document of the nature of which the will was executed by the testator. The will was not a valid will but was a valid will, and the High Court had rightly held that the document was not a genuine document. The High power of attorney was not a deed of conveyance and the will was a valid document. The will did not create any right in the property. The will had not been proved by the testator and the will had not proved its execution. The High Judgment of the High Court is set aside. The High judgment of the High court is restored.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Brahmins of Manjakollai village in the year 1957. The appellant was elected to the office of a trustee by a member of the Sengunta community. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the trusteeship of the appellant was not hereditary. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The appellant contended that the succession was not hereditary and that the right to the office was not hereditary in the sense that on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the office as a matter of course, because the successor acquires a right only by appointment and the authority to appoint is vested in the assembly of the bairagis and the worshippets. Held, that the appellant is a hereditary trustee within the meaning of the section. The right to the post of trustee in the present case was not hereditary within the meaning Of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The appellant 's right to the appointment of the trustee in the instant case was not a hereditary right. The right of the appellant to the office in question was not hereditary, because the office of the appellant being hereditary, the suit was for a fixed period of one year and not for life. The appellant had a right only 'by appointment and the authorities were right in holding that the office of trustee in a hereditary office was not a post abolished. The appellant could not succeed to his office as a hereditary trustee. The appellant is not a hereditary trustee but a hereditary trustee, because his office is a hereditary office. The appellant cannot succeed to his own office. The office of the trustee is for a fixed duration of one year. The appellant, therefore, was a hereditary office within the meaning. of section 6(1) of the Act.

The appellant was a trade union officer. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, and in two of the three appeals, he was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant was convicted and convicted under section 52. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was restricted to the acquittal of the appellant in respect of offences under section 411 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three cases. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 411 of Indian Penal Code, as the appellant had not been convicted under section 411. Held, that the appellant could not be convicted under section 414 of the Indian Evidence Act, because, he had the opportunity to obtain the articles seized from the house in which the articles were seized. The appellant had the opportunity of obtaining the articles from the post office and had the opportunity, to get the articles seized, to be in the possession of the appellant. The appellant could not, therefore, be convicted under the section. The appellant must be deemed to be in exclusive possession of the articles seized. The fact that the articles were found in the almirah was not a circumstance which would justify the inference that the almirah were in the possession and possession of the respondent. The appellant, therefore, could not be held guilty under section 411 Of the Indian Penal code. The appellant has not been convicted for the offence under section 411 but has been convicted for an offence under section 414. The appellant is entitled to the protection of section 411 Of Indian Penal Code and the appellant must be held to be in possession of the almirah in the manner prescribed by section 411 Of that Code. The appellant cannot be convicted under that section. The fact of the almirahs being in the possession or possession of the person who was in possession of a almirah which was in his exclusive possession does not make the prosecution case against the appellant.

The respondents, who were the owners of coal mines, were granted coal and coal mining rights in respect of the coal mines. The appellant 's case was that as a result of a letter written by the Inspector of Mines to the respondents, the respondents had encroached upon the coal mines and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portion and had rendered it ineffective. The respondents contended that the appellant had encroached upon their coal mines and that the respondents had not taken any steps to remove the coal from the encroached portion. The Subordinate Judge held that the respondents were bound to keep a barrier of 25 feet to the south of the respondent 's working and that the appellant was not entitled to any damages. The Subordinate judge held that the appellant 's action was not bona fide and that the respondent had no knowledge of the appellant ' 's encroachment of their coal mines. On appeal the High Court held that the respondent was not entitled under the Rules to the exemption. Held, that the respondents could not be allowed to take advantage of the fact that the appellant did not take any steps to prevent the respondents from encroaching upon the coal mine and that the coal that was left in the encroached portion was not by any means accessible to the appellant and was wholly unworkable. The respondents had knowledge of the fact of the appellant having encroached upon the appellant '. The respondents were not entitled to the exemption and the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the exemption. The appellant had no knowledge that the respondents 's encroachment was due to the fact that they had encroached upon any portion of their coal mine. The respondents could not, therefore, be allowed to raise the plea of limitation.

The appellant, a company, entered into an agreement with the respondents, that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award, and the respondents, an award, had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day. The respondents, however, contended that the appellant was not entitled to the payment of the wages authority, and that the respondents were not barred by limitation. The respondents contested the claim. The respondents raised two pleas, namely, (1) that the appellant had not been given the minimum wage as defined by section 2(vi) of the Act, and (2) that the respondents had not been able to establish that the appellant 's wages were not wages under section 2(v) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and (3) that the award was not made by the Industrial Tribunal. [434 C] (3) The appellant 's contention that the respondents should be paid wages under section 10 of the Act before it was amended, was not accepted by the High Court. The appellant, a public limited company, was carrying on business in the erstwhile State of Travancore. The Travancore Act, 1950, provided that the business of the company was to be carried on by a company in the State of Travancore and that the company was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that State. The appellant was a public limited Company incorporated in the State. The business of the appellant was to carry on business in Travancore State. The income of the appellant, in the assessment year 1950 51, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The appellant claimed that the income of the company being the same as the profits of the company, the same should be deducted from the profits of its business. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The appellant 's appeal to the Appellate Tribunal was unsuccessful but the Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax, it was entitled to deduction of the losses incurred in the previous year in the previous years. The High Court in reference, held that the company had no business loss in the previous accounting year and that the loss of the company could not be deducted from its profits. Held, that the company being a public limited limited company, the profits of which were exempted from payment of tax in British India were not liable to be deducted from profits of the previous year. The business in the present case was to be assessed to income of the previous years and not to the income of a company. The business was one and indivisible and the profits of a company were exempt from tax in British territory. The business could not be said to be one and indivisible, for the purpose was to be taxed in British India. The business which was to be taken into account was to be the business of a company in which the company was carrying on the business and the profits were to be deducted therefrom. The business carried on by the company was one and the same as it was carrying on its business.

The appellant contended that the age fixed by the Tribunal was not correct and that the Tribunal had not taken into consideration the fact that the age was fixed at 60 and the age fixed was not unreasonable. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the age could not be fixed at 55 and that the tribunal had not taken any other view of the matter. The Tribunal had not considered the question whether it should be fixed on the basis of the age of the employees of the respondent company or whether it should have fixed the retirement age at 60. It was not correct to say that the age had to be raised to 58 and that it was open to the Tribunal to consider the question whether the age of compulsory retirement should be fixed in the light of the decision of this Court in the case of the Bombay region. The Tribunal was right. The Tribunal has not considered the evidence on record and has come to the conclusion that the age has to be raised at 55. The Tribunal 's conclusion that the retirement of the respondent workmen should be raised before the Tribunal was correct. The Tribunal, therefore, was right in taking the view that the age at 55 should be raised and that the retirement should be made on the basis that the age is raised to 60. The fact that in the Bombay region at least there is a general agree ment that the age will be raised to 55 and that in the present case the age of retire should be raised. The Tribunal therefore had to consider the matter afresh and decide the question whether in the circumstances of the case the age should not be raised to the age of 60.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine. The High Court and the Court below were of the opinion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits and were convicted under sections 395 and 395 of the Penal Code and were sentenced to 5 year ' rigorous imprisonment. The High court and the Court were of the view that the appellants had been convicted under section 396 of the Indian and sentenced them to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the presumption under section 114 of the has been rebutted by the evidence of the witnesses who were examined in the case and that the presumption could not be drawn against the appellants. HELD : (i) The presumption under section 113 of the Evidence Act is not a presumption in favour of the accused and the presumption under that section is not a rebuttable one. The presumption under that Section is not a weak one and the presumption that the accused was concerned with the crime itself gets weakened. [725 F G] (ii) The presumption that the appellants are the dacoits is stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed. The reason is obvious. disposal of the fruits, of crime requires the finding of a person ready to receive them and the shortness of time, the nature of the property which is disposed of, that is to say, its quantity and its character determined whether the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit. In other cases the presumption can be drawn only when the circumstances show that the accused had been concerned in the commission of the crime. [726 F G]

The appellant was detained under the impugned order of detention on the 8th June 1955, and was in detention for more than three years. The grounds of detention were vague. The grounds were vague and the grounds of detention mentioned only the grounds of non disclosure. The grounds did not indicate the grounds of the detention. The appellant was arrested on the 9th June 1954, and was detained under section 3 of the . The grounds of his detention were vague and did not indicate any grounds of detention. The grounds showed that the grounds of his arrest were vague and that the grounds were vague. Held, that the grounds did not disclose the grounds of grounds of detention and the grounds did no show that the grounds for non disclosure were vague. It was not necessary for the detaining authority to apply its mind to the existence or otherwise of the grounds of deten tion. The grounds could not be said to have prejudiced the detenu in any way. The grounds for non compliance with the grounds of preventive detention were vague, and the grounds were not vague. The order of detention was mala fide. The last two had been urged before the detaining authority and the grounds showed that there was no ground for non disclosure. Held, further, that the order of detention did not disclose any ground of detention. It was a case of mere non disclosure of facts which were not communicated to the detenue at the time of the detention, and the order of non disclosure was not mala fide. It was open to the detenu to make a representation to the detaining authority against the order of preventive detention. The order was mala fide and the grounds could not therefore be said to be vague. The fact that the detenue was furnished information, at the time when the grounds were furnished, was not sufficient to justify the non disclosure.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants and the appellants were put in possession of the mills and the factory. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari to quash the notice and the writ of certiorari issued by the High Court. The appellants contended that the respondent had no authority to sell the mills and that the respondent was not entitled to cancel the lease in their favour, and that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of the Act. Held, that the respondent could not be said to have been acting within his authority in issuing the notice under section 12 of the Act, and that it was not necessary for the respondent to have issued the notice in question under section 12. The section expressly authorised the custodian to cancel the notice and to make a fresh notice. The section was intended to be retrospective in operation and it was not intended to affect the rights of the appellants in the matter of the lease. The section did not confer any authority on the custodian to cancellation the lease in favour of the appellants. The section merely authorised the custodian, to cancel the agreement, and the respondent could be said to be acting within his powers in issuing the lease. It was not necessary to make a reference to the section. The section clearly intended to repel a possible contention that section 12 did not by implication repeal statutes confer rights on lessees, and cannot be reconciled with the contention of the appellants that it conferred no authority on him to cancel the contract. The section further stated that the power to cancel a lease may be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". The section expressly authorises the custodian to vary the terms of the lease, and the section does not confer any power on the custodian or the Custodian to cancel the same. The section does not authorise the custodian to revoke the lease in his favour. The section only provides that the custodian may cancel the lease if he is satisfied that the lease is not in accordance with the terms of a lease. The respondent was acting within his power in issuing the notices under section 12 and the appellants had no authority under section 12 to cancel the said lease in their absence. The section also does not authorise any such authority to cancel the order of the Custodian. The section, therefore, did not authorise the Custodian to revoke the notice in his favour, and the appellants could not be asked to cancel the notices.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu, which was a clerk. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975 a resolution was passed by the Panchayat Samitis to the effect that the appellant should be absorbed as a Head clerk on an adhoc basis. The appellant was confirmed in the post in course on April 1, 1975. On April 1,1975 the appellant was appointed temporarily as Head Clerk on a permanent basis. On April l, 1975 the appellant, was confirmed in his post in course. On April 25, 1975, the appellant was promoted as Head Clerk. On April 28, 1975 he was confirmed in service. On April 30, 1975 his services were regularised as a Head Cashier. On April 27, 1975 another resolution was passed to the effect, that the appellant would be absorbed as Head Clerk in the Government service on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayat. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court, challenging the validity of the Amending Act of 1973. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that by reason of section 14(4) of the Amending act, the appellant had become entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same conditions on which they were employed by the Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The appointment of the appellant to the post of a Head Clerk being without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post of the Head Clerk. He was appointed lawfully to the post, and that is the post in which the Government had absorbed him. [727F] The appellant was entitled to be absorbed as the Head Clerk on the date on which it purported to do so. [728G]

The appellants were the trustees of the Math and the deity. The suit properties were described by the Mahant in the following terms: "Godge, sovereigns and gold besides two fixed deposits with the Bank of Bengal of Rs. 45,000. " The appellants were the chela of Mahant Shivshankar Yati and the appellants were the Mahant and Sarbarakar. The appellants were in possession of the properties as Mahant and Sarjashankar Yati. The appellants filed a suit claiming that the properties in question belonged to the Math and that the trustees were in possession thereof. The suit was contested by the appellants. The High Court held in favour of appellants. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellants had no right to claim exemption from the payment of the tax. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The income from the properties in dispute was the income derived from the properties of the Math. The income derived from these properties was the income from the property of the Math, and therefore, the income derived therefrom was the income. [681F] (2) The income derived by the Math and not the income from property of the temple was the income of the Math or the deity. [682G] (3) The income of the properties in the present case was the income which was the income, derived from the property. The income was the income and not the property of a Math or the temple. [683G] (4) The income was not the income of a Math nor was it the income of any other person. [684A] (5) The income which was derived from the Math or temple was the personal property of the Mahant. [685B] (6) The income received by the Mahant from the properties was the personal income of the Mahant and not the properties of a Math. [686C] (7) The income, derived by the Mahant, was the income received by him from the properties. The income, therefore, was the personal and property of the trustee. [687E] (7)(a) The income in the present cases was the income accruing from the properties as the income was the personal properties of the Mahant, and not the personal property. The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of the village panchayats in 1949 and the land allotted to them in substitution of the lands at evacuees was given quasi permanent allotment in another village. The appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General, Evacuee Property, but the Additional Custodian for the State of Punjab cancelled the allotment of the lands in favour of the appellants. The Additional Custodian, however, dismissed the revision application on the ground that the appellants were not entitled to allotment of suburban land. The appellants preferred an appeal to the Custodian General. The Custodian General, however, allowed the appeal on the ground of delay and cancelled the allotment. The appellants appealed to the Custodian, who dismissed the appeal on merits. The Custodian, however dismissed the revision on the ground, inter alia, that the appellants had no locus standi to file the revision application. The appellants then filed a revision petition before the Custodian, which was dismissed. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the Custodian General was right in holding that the appellants could not make out a new case at this stage of argument. The appellants were not precluded from challenging the order of cancellation of the allotment in their favour by the Custodian General on the ground inter alia that the order of the Custodian was not a transfer of the property of the appellants to the manager and therefore could not be said to be an order of cancellation. The order of the Additional Custodian was not an order of the Deputy Custodian. The order was not a mere order of cancellation but was a mere order by the Custodian. The Custodian was not competent to cancel the allotment in favour of any one else. The order did not amount to a transfer of property of the appellant to the manager. The order could not be challenged on the ground only that it was an order of transfer of property. The order, however, did not amount either to a transfer or to a transfer. The order merely stated that the order was to be made by the Custodian and not to a transfer and it was not a case of cancellation of an allotment. The order does not amount to an order of a transfer of land. The order is not a mere an order of allotment but a mere order for the purpose of making an order of confirmation. The order must be a mere order or an order of an allotment and not a mere one. The order in the present case was not a sale of land but a transfer of a property in the compensation pool. The order made by the Additional Custodian on the ground merely stated that he was not a party to the proceedings before the Custodian. Held, further, that the order did not create any right in the appellants to make the allotment of land. Held, also, that the orders of the Additional Director of Evacuee Property, Evacuee Property and the Additional Custodian were not final and could not be questioned in the proceedings before him. The order passed by the Additional Director was not a final order of the evacuee property and was not a nullity.

Held, that the words " a registered dealer" in section 10(d) of the Bombay Act, as a " registered dealer" and " an unregistered dealer" in the Act, were wide enough to include a registered dealer or anybody else. The words " a person " in section 10 (b) of that Act were wide enough, to include a " registered dealers" and the purchasing dealers were liable to pay purchase tax under the section. The words, " a registered person" in section 8 were wide enough but the words "registered dealer" in s.10(b) meant " a registered dealers" or a person who is not a registered dealer. The words are wide enough to cover registered dealer and an unregistered dealer. The word " registered" in section 12(b) is wide enough to comprehend registered dealers and an unregistered person. The trial court, however, held that the respondent was a subsisting marriage and that the appellant had by virtue of the compromise become the absolute owner of the flat and various deposits in respect of the said flat. The trial Court, however, found that the appellant and the respondent were not subsisting and that the respondent had no subsisting relationship with the appellant and that the marriage was not performed in accordance with the customary or personal law. The High Court, however held that the marriage between the appellant and respondent was not a subsisting marriage. The respondent was not liable to pay the maintenance under the said section. The appellant could claim maintenance under that section only if the respondent was alive and was not alive. [81 E] (7) The appellant is not entitled to the maintenance under Section 125. The State legislature was competent to pass the law, and the State Legislature was not competent to pass a law with regard to the matters covered by the Act of the State. The appellant, a lessee of a private land, was notified under section 3 of the Madras Estate (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, to be a lessee of the land. The appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Rajah to him. The Collector, on the same day, granted a lease for twenty years to the appellant. On the expiry of the fifth year, the Rajah granted a lease to the appellant for a period of 20 years commencing from February 1, 1947, and ending on November 30, 1947. On December 10, 1947 the appellant applied to be confirmed by the Rajah on the ground that the lease was not a lease within the meaning of the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The appellant contended that the lease could not be terminated by the Government, and that the lease had been terminated by the State Government on December 10,1947, and that it was not a case of a lease within section 20(2) of the Act. Held, that the lease in question was not a 'lease ' within the meaning Of section 20(3) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and conversion into Ryotwar) Act, 1938, and was not a "lease" within the meaning ofs.20(1) Of the Act. The second proviso to the section, which is a self contained proviso, is not a self contained provision and the aid of the third proviso is wholly uncalled for. The second Proviso to the section is not a " lease" within the definition of the term in section 20(4) of the Mines Act, 1952. The second and third proviso deal with the termination of rights created after July 1, 1945, and the second proviso deals with the termination by the Government of the lease. The second part of the proviso deals with a situation where the Government has no power to terminate the lease and the lessee has no right to terminate the rights created after the lease is determined under the second proviso. The second, proviso deals with termination of rights in anticipation of the impending legislation and hence it is not a lease.
